title: The subject of the sentence and expressing desire
summary: Japanese happily lets things be the main carriage, so "I like coffee" is really "coffee is pleasing". The same logic explains ほしい, たい and たがる.

blocks.text: English wants a person, usually "I", to be the actor of every sentence. Japanese is happy to put a **thing** in the main carriage. This explains the sentences that confuse learners most.

One idea runs through the whole lesson: **particles always point the same way**, like a compass needle pointing north. が always marks the main carriage and never the object, even when English would call the thing "the object".
"I like coffee" is not about I

Look where が sits: on the **coffee**. 好きだ means "is pleasing", so the sentence says "coffee is pleasing". "I" is only the **topic**: the one who feels it. Textbooks that say が marks "the object" here teach you something that never happens.
The main carriage is コーヒー. 好き is a な-type word meaning "pleasing".
Another word that works the same way is **わかる**: "is understandable / clear". The thing understood is the main carriage.

blocks.en: The book is understandable. (I understand the book.)

blocks.text: **ほしい** is an い-adjective meaning "is wanted". The thing wanted is the main carriage. The wish itself belongs to the speaker, so it is not written.
（私は）子猫がほしい。 A kitten is wanted.

blocks.en: (I) want a kitten. (A kitten is wanted.)

blocks.text: To want to **do** something, attach the adjective **たい** to the **い-stem** of the verb. To make the **い-stem**: an ichidan verb drops **る** (食べる → 食べ), and a godan verb changes its last kana to the **い** row (飲む → 飲み). Then add **たい**.
Again the thing is the main carriage: "crepes are eating-desired".
私はクレープが食べたい。

blocks.jp: 私はクレープが食べたい。

blocks.text: When nothing is marked with が, the zero is the speaker: the engine is about "I".
Feeling words like **怖い** can have the feeler or the cause as the carriage. If the thing is the carriage, it means "is scary"; with nothing named, it means the speaker feels it.

blocks.en: Ghosts are scary. (I am scared of ghosts.)

blocks.text: Feelings of other people: がる

Words like ほしい, たい and 怖い describe a feeling **from the inside**: the speaker's. They cannot describe someone else's feelings, because you cannot see them. For other people, attach **がる** ("shows signs of") to the stem. がる makes a **verb**, because all you can see is behavior. And because it is now a verb, the thing wanted takes **を**, as with any verb.
The particle switches: ほしい takes が, ほしがる takes を.

blocks.jp: さくらがケーキを欲しがる。
blocks.en: Sakura wants cake. (she shows signs of wanting it)

blocks.jp: さくらが猫をほしがっている。
blocks.en: Sakura wants a cat. (the natural form is ている)

blocks.title: Remember
items: **が** marks the main carriage even in **好きだ**, **ほしい**, **たい** and **わかる**.
**ほしい**: "is wanted" (い-adjective). **い-stem + たい**: "is desired to do".
Feelings from the inside belong to the **speaker**; for someone else, add **がる**, which makes a verb that takes **を**.
The topic (**私は**) is only the one who feels it.

questions.note: 好きだ describes the thing: it is the main carriage.

questions.prompt: 私は新しい自転車＿＿ほしい。
questions.note: The thing wanted is the main carriage.
たい makes the thing the main carriage.
わかる treats the thing as the main carriage.

questions.note: For someone else, がる shows signs of wanting.
questions.en: My younger sister wants a new bag.

questions.note: For another person, attach がる to たい.
questions.en: My older brother wants to drink water.
